thread.title: Is Capital Spending Picking Up? Will This Result In Faster Economic Growth?

author: John M. Mason
title: Is Capital Spending Picking Up? Will This Result In Faster Economic Growth?
text:
Data provided by Credit Suisse is indicating that business capital investment expenditures are picking up.
"Spending on factories, equipment and other capital goods by companies in the S&P 500 is expected to have risen to $166 billion in the first quarter, up 24 percent from a year earlier," reports the Wall Street Journal .
"It is on track for the fastest pickup since 2011 and a record for the first quarter of a year." This is just the kind of news economists have been waiting for.
Consumption spending has driven the current economic recovery. The Federal Reserve System under the leadership of former chairman Ben Bernanke explicitly set out to create a wealth effect that would stimulate consumer expenditures and get the economy growing again following the end of the Great Recession.
Although the efforts of Mr. Bernanke and the Fed can be considered to be successful as the economy has lasted almost nine full years and has become the second longest economic recovery on record. Yet, the compound annual rate of growth achieved over this time period has only been 2.2 percent, the lowest rate of growth achieved overall in any economic recovery.
What has been missing, many economists have claimed, has been business capital spending.
The slow rate of growth achieved in this recovery, it is argued, has been because capital spending has not produced the conditions for improvement in labor productivity, which has only been modestly above zero since the beginning of the recovery.
Had there been more capital spending, productivity growth would have been greater, and economic growth would have been more rapid, and perhaps, there would have been a greater rise in wages.
Therefore, it is hoped that the pickup in capital investment expenditures, attributed to the tax reform bill passed by Congress in December 2017, will be the stimulus the economy needs to not only continue to grow, after all this time of recovery, but to also speed up the rate at which it is growing.
But it is not at all certain that the increase in capital investment expenditures will have this positive impact on growth rates.
The Wall Street Journal article, after discussing the increase that is reported to have taken place in the first quarter of 2018, goes on to present another issue.
"Data suggest that shares of companies with large and growing capex tend to underperform the broader stock market-which could weigh on returns just as the market has become more volatile."
"Shares of the 20 companies in the S&P 500 that spent most on capex (capital expenditures) in the first quarter are up 0.5 percent for the year, trailing the broad index's 1.4 percent gain…."
"The trend becomes even more pronounced over longer time horizons. Since 1986, companies with the highest capex-to-sales ratios have underperformed the S&P 500 by more than 2 percentage points on average each year, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch."
With this kind of a result, one could strongly argue that the companies with the highest capex-to-sales are not getting a sufficient return on their invested capital relative to the cost of capital. As a consequence, the stock prices of these companies are not performing well relative to the other companies in the S&P 500 index.
The article refers to research that has specifically found that "companies that have the biggest increases in capital spending have subsequently had underperforming stock returns."
Maybe, however, the situation that we are facing is that the nature of industry is changing. Maybe… just, maybe… the factors contributing the most to corporate financial outcomes these days have changed.
Recently, I have written about " Apple, The Epitome Of Where The Modern Corporation Is Going ." Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) "perhaps represents what the modern corporate world is all about…both industrial companies and financial companies."
Before talking about why Apple might be different, let me just add that this company earned a 36.1 percent rate of return on shareholders' equity in 2017 and that its worst performance in recent years was the 20.5 percent ROE it achieved in 2009. Economists would argue that it has a sustainable competitive advantage.
And what are the meaningful things Apple does that others need to emulate? First, Apple "is an expert in financial engineering." This is very important in this age of credit inflation where corporations must take advantage of the environment that the government underwrites and sustains.
Second, Apple "is a leader in the use of intangibles like intellectual property and brands relative to tangible goods." More importantly, "intellectual property is extremely scalable and enjoys network effects."
Third, the environment Apple operates within "lends itself more to mergers and acquisitions that accelerate the concentration of power in these corporations." This is, of course, another part of financial engineering.
It is not that capital spending is not increasing within the tech space, but that the capital spending is being incorporated within the primary focus of those companies inhabiting the digital universe. The Wall Street Journal article discusses how Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN ) has incorporated capital spending within its delivery network and capital offerings.
But this gets into other aspect of these "new" companies. For one, there is the use of big data to know customers better and to build better offerings. Then there is the changing idea of ownership as many of the digital companies offer subscription services, and this applies to physical goods like cars, leasing arrangements creating a continuing relationship with customers, different payment structures and services, and then there are streaming services. The push here seems to be to achieve "the end of ownership."
It seems as the fundamentals of economic growth have changed and have taken corporations more and more away from buying and building on physical capital investment. What this seems to be telling us is that "heavy industry and manufacturing" is not what drives the world today.
As a consequence, therefore, we need to look at the organizations, like Apple and Amazon and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), and ask what it is that is driving them. Digital growth may be nothing like manufacturing growth. If so, maybe we need to change our perception of what drives the economy.
